Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Health Sciences is a rapidly changing and evolving discipline, requiring highly trained, critical thinkers to solve some of society’s biggest health-related problems. The Ph.D. in Health Sciences is a college-wide degree with faculty from multiple departments/programs in the College of Health Sciences and focuses on health, wellness, and quality of life across the lifespan. Research brings together faculty and students to solve important health-related problems through a mix of basic, applied and translational science. The program allows students the opportunity to gain experience in the various disciplines that make up health sciences and provides them with the opportunity for advanced content knowledge and in- depth training in one discipline or area of study.

Students are eligible to apply for this program after earning a post-baccalaureate degree in a health-related field. Physical Therapy was not initially included as a specialization because the graduate catalog language (which has now been changed) required a master’s degree to have 30 credits from their post-baccalaureate degree apply to their doctoral program. Physical Therapy does not offer a master's degree. Instead, students in this discipline go on to the

doctoral of physical therapy (DPT).
Therefore, no credits from the DPT would count toward the PhD.
The graduate council approved language (Nov. 9, 2020) in the graduate manual to let students with a master’s or qualifying graduate degree request up to 30 credits from this degree to be applied to their doctoral program.
This includes the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) degree.
Given this change, we would like to add Physical Therapy as a specialization to the CHS doctoral program.
The sub-plan for DPT would be as follows:  CHS Core o 9 credits in health (CHS 601, 605, 610) o 6 credits in statistics from approved list (above) o 3 credits in research methods from approved list (above)  PHT Sub-Plansubplan Course Work o minimum of 42 credits selected with advisor to ensure disciplinary expertise; 6 of these credits must be in courses related to physical therapy  Doctoral Dissertation Research o PHT 699 (12 18 credits) 6.

Priority Items (40 minutes) 3.1 New ‘home’ for the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Graduate Programs - The three INP graduate programs (MS, PhD and Certificate) were administratively re-homed from the Graduate School to CHS as a result of the December senate meeting.
Senate officers have heard inquiries and concerns about that move and it appears that a process improvement should be implemented that might ensure program directors are not left out of these decisions.

There were questions about the origins of such proposals and why the system is built in such a way that deans can leapfrog relevant faculty.
Beyond the mechanics of Kuali proposals, there seems to be a need to develop a better model for how interdisciplinary programs are housed at the university.
Pres.
Williams will try to learn more about the genesis of this particular change and the approval process it was subjected to.
FSEC may circle back with tangible suggestions for process improvements but in the meantime, staff was asked to pay particular attention to “administrative” requests in Kuali and alert the FSEC or senate officers to any concerns.
Sen.
Trimm will communicate with CASC about how to approach such proposals, if necessary, and VP Preisser will do the same with the Graduate Council. 3.2 Future Legislation Updates i.
Establishing College Liaisons - The FSEC Officers are meeting with the Council of Deans next week (2/4) and hope to gather their input and use it to refine the draft. ii.
College By-Laws - This remains a secondary priority behind the Liaisons.
FSEC members agree that once the liaison roles are established and liaisons start meeting together, 1

shared information about the disparate operations of the colleges will help make a case for a By-laws mandate or other common governance structure requirements. iii.
Chapter 8 amendments related to 7 & 14 week calendar alignment - VP Preisser provided a synopsis of the plan to roll out a four program pilot of concurrent enrollment options in Fall, 2027.
The affected colleges will need to vote in favor of the plan in order for it to go forward.
The pilot will be subject to review and renewal at the end of four years.
If the Senate elects to reject renewal, the concurrent enrollments will end at the conclusion of the spring, 2031 term.
If the senate determines that the system is working well, the initiative could be expanded.
Questions were asked about the basis for renewal and if expectations can and will be set for a meaningful evaluation.
There was also a concern about institutional memory given that senators sitting at roll-out will cycle off the senate prior to the renewal phase.
VP Preisser noted that it will be up to the programs themselves to initiate their renewal so the senate will not need to ‘remember’ to do it.

A final draft is expected today and FSEC agreed to forward it to TAAC, CBUM and the ACC for review.
The legislation will be introduced in February and docketed for action in March, if ready. iv.
Clarifying and specifying launch date for SGO and 4+ attempt legislation - Staff is preparing amendments to FSEC Bills 4 and 5 to include the effective dates (Fall 2026) and will ensure that future bills all include an effective date. v.
Approval of academic calendars 8 years in advance - The Graduate School has expressed a need to set the calendar eight years in advance and such a change would require amending Sec. 8.70.10 of the UM, which prescribes a 6-year calendar.
This move would temporarily add to the workload of the ACC, which would be tasked with preparing and presenting for approval two additional calendars all in one year.
The Committee is responsible for setting the Summer, Online, standard academic year calendars, including J-term, but would need to close the gap between the 6- and 8- years out versions.
The amendment itself is straightforward and could be introduced in February. vi.

Adjusting due date for final grades - There are concerns about the timelines associated with faculty entering final grades after exams, academic standing notifications being generated, and students having adequate time to react to those notifications, especially if they need to file a grade appeal or are facing a negative finding regarding their academic standing.
URI faculty often benefit from ample time to report grades, but sometimes face quicker turnarounds.
The administration recently suggested running an AI model to determine a standard that might be optimal for students,faculty, and advising staff.
FSEC members suggested that no such effort is likely necessary, because a quick look at the due dates for the last four years reveals that faculty have not faced a deadline earlier than six days post-exam.
It would be simple and probably agreeable to simply establish that time frame as a standard.
There was some concern about the fall semester in particular, since the deadline could bump up against the Christmas holiday.
Pres.

Williams revealed that Fannon Institute Director Kim Stack has done some research on this matter and found that at most peer institutions, the norm for grade posting is 72 hours after the exam is completed.
It will be important to emphasize that the time of the staff involved in generating the standing reports is valuable too, and a balance needs to be struck between faculty preferences and the needs of staff to generate adequate and timely reports that serve students’ needs. 2

3.3 Missing Classroom Database (circling back) - Pres.
Williams reported that he has communicated with the JCSC and the CTI about the initiative to restore the database as a resource.
It is hoped that they will make substantial progress before the end of the academic year. 3.4 Campus restrooms/Washrooms/Religious observances (circling back) - Pres.
Williams noted the database of single user facilities has been updated as a web resource but it does not provide any intersection with accessible facilities.
This still needs to happen.
It was also recently noted that washroom needs related to cultural and religious practices should likely be addressed but this would be an extensive project with multiple stakeholders.
It does not appear the senate has the bandwidth to tackle it this year so VP Preisser was encouraged to keep it on his radar for next year. 3.5 Advance Planning - 2/19/26 FS meeting - The agenda was reviewed and a suggestion was made about adding the 7 & 14 week calendar alignment language.

FSEC still has another week before it needs to approve the agenda for posting. 3.6 Advance Planning - AY 26-27 FS meeting schedule - It was noted recently that this year’s confluence of an FSEC meeting, the first day of classes and a senate meeting proved to be a lot for many faculty.
Staff offered a calendar draft for next year so that FSEC has the opportunity to weigh all options before presenting something to the senate.
The current draft attempts to standardize the third Thursday each month, consistent with the Manual, and takes into account all religious holidays when work is not permitted. 3.7 Senate role in approving a new institute (CHILD Institute) - The CIRC has approved the creation of a new Institute.
Committee Liaison Meenach will ask the Chair of CIRC to prepare a brief report for the next Senate meeting and attach all supporting documents so the senate might review it as required. 3.8 MPS rehoming (circling back) - Pres.
Williams reached out to the departments involved in the Program to gain feedback on the re-homing to the College of Education from the Graduate School.
There seemed to be some misunderstanding of how the budget model works.

It requires that the “money follows the instructor” which means that the departments will keep revenue for their courses and those funds will not be diverted to the CoEdu.
But there does seem to be opacity around the administrative apparatus.
The college is simply responsible for ‘stacking’ the certificates that the departments offer, and will likely get to count the graduates in their degree conferral numbers.
It remains unclear how those numbers factor in as KPIs under the budget model, so the move could still have a budgetary impact even though the direct course revenue path is well-defined.
FSEC will need to monitor in an ongoing way and be mindful of any other administrative changes that are proposed, as they could have similar unpredictable consequences. 4.

It does not have to be the only avenue available to students but does need to be an option.
Although there have been well-known delays and complications in the bookstore securing 3

materials, the alternatives pursued by faculty in lieu of the bookstore can easily become a logistical and ethical minefield.
Concerns were expressed that the current bookstore retailer has attempted to force faculty to standardize course materials across all sections of a given course and this is a serious infringement of faculty rights.
The FS Pres. and VP met earlier with the Student Senate President who voiced a concern that textbook affordability has become a serious issue for undergraduates.
Federal mandates around student aid use make bookstore cooperation even more important.
That being said, the APC is about to update its Textbook and Course Materials Policy and has asked the FSEC officers and other volunteers to serve as reviewers; Sens.
